headline: Twotree Albies Showed Up Right on Cue — Bunker Blitzes Building Off Black Point
subhead: The fall push finally hit Eastern CT waters this week, with false albacore working Twotree Channel and stripers stacking under bunker from Niantic Bay to Hole-in-the-Wall.
body_markdown:
Talk at the Niantic docks this week has been all albies, and for good reason. The mates coming off the afternoon runs out of Waterford have been seeing surface activity off Twotree Island Channel that wasn't there ten days ago — hard, fast boils pushing bait up and small torpedo-shaped fish crashing through it. We flagged this last week, said to watch for albie numbers to build in this zone as the warm-water push worked west out of Rhode Island, and that's exactly what's happening. Fishers Island Sound sits right at our doorstep, and when that false albacore and bonito bite gets rolling out there, it doesn't take long to show up on our side of the line.

The bigger story right now, though, is bunker. The Harvest Moon tides this week have put real muscle behind the tide swings, and that's dragging peanut and adult menhaden schools through the inlets and along the beaches on a schedule you can set a watch to. New London is reading around 69.4 degrees, still comfortably warm for this time of year, while the water out toward the Race and the western Sound is running a couple degrees warmer than that. That gradient matters — it's kept the bait active and moving instead of locking up, and the stripers and bluefish know it. Anywhere bunker gets squeezed against structure — Black Point, the rocks off McCook Point, the mouth of the Niantic River — you're going to find bass and blues working underneath and behind the pods.

Striper fishing has been the more dependable half of the week. The pattern the fleet is leaning on is straightforward: find the bunker schools getting pushed by current against Black Point or piling up in the deeper cuts of Twotree Channel, then work bucktails or big soft plastics — 6-inch white or bunker-colored paddletails on 1- to 1.5-ounce jig heads — right under the edges of the school. Fish are holding a little deeper than the surface blitzes suggest, often 15 to 25 feet down even when the bunker are getting hammered up top, so give the jig a few extra seconds to sink before you start the retrieve. Live-lining a bunker on a fish-finder rig off Hole-in-the-Wall has also been paying off on the stronger tide stages, particularly the first two hours of the outgoing when the current really starts moving bait out of the bay. Sizes have been a mixed bag — plenty of schoolies in the mid-20-inch range mixed with occasional fish pushing into slot territory, nothing gigantic yet, but that should change as more forage stacks up with these bigger Harvest Moon tides over the next week or two.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on nearly every bunker blitz right now, same as everywhere else along the coast this month. They've been the more aggressive player at first light off McCook Point and around the river mouth, blowing up on topwater plugs and metal — Kastmasters and 1-ounce Deadly Dicks have both been getting bit hard when the blues push bait to the surface. If you want bluefish specifically, work the edges of the bass activity; they'll usually show up first and loudest.

Fluke have held up better than you'd expect for late September, and that's a direct function of the warmer water lingering in the bay. Niantic Bay itself and the flats off McCook Point are still giving up keeper-class fluke on the drift, with Gulp Swimming Mullets in white or pink on 3/4-ounce bucktails doing the damage in 20 to 30 feet of water on the last of the incoming tide. It won't last — any real cold front that drops water temps sharply will start tightening this bite up fast, so if fluke is the target, the next week or so is the window rather than a sure thing into October.

Black sea bass are holding their own on the structure they always hold on this time of year — the rock piles off Black Point and the deeper humps around Twotree — and that bite has been steady rather than spectacular. Squid strips and clam on standard sea bass rigs in 30 to 40 feet is still producing a mixed bag with enough keepers to make the stops worthwhile. Blackfish are starting to show interest as well, with a few early reports of tautog coming off crab baits worked tight to structure, a sign that the fall pattern for that fishery is beginning to kick in a little ahead of schedule.

Looking at the next several days, the Harvest Moon tides should keep bait moving hard and keep the bass and blues concentrated at the structure and inlets where that bait gets funneled. The albie window is the one to watch closest — if the warm filament pushing west from Rhode Island holds its line, expect Twotree and the mouth of Fishers Island Sound to keep producing, maybe even build, over the coming week. The wildcard is any real cooling trend; a hard cold front would start squeezing the fluke bite first and could push the bigger migratory stripers through faster rather than settling them in. For now, the smart play is working the tide changes at Black Point and Hole-in-the-Wall early and evaluating the albie situation at Twotree once you're out there — the fleet's finding them, but it's still a moving target from day to day.
